title: Kestrel Commerce - POC weekly throughput sync
summary: Weekly POC sync to review last 72h throughput runs, validate continuous batching adjustments, re-baseline concurrency targets, and agree next steps for weekend stress test. Observed improved steady-state RPS with higher tail latency on cold cache. Agreed to lower queue depth and raise concurrency ceiling per GPU for short prompts.
topics: continuous batching adjustments and buffer sizing
KV cache hit rate and prefix caching
next steps: weekend stress test, runbook update, pricing note

Aria to confirm stakeholder availability for go/no-go on Aug 18

transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-08-10 09:30 PDT | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Maya Chen, Liam Patel, Noah Rivera (Redwood) — Aria Gomez, Samir Rao, Lena Ortiz, Diego Park (Kestrel)

[00:00] Maya Chen: ok hi everyone thanks for joining.. reading on time. this is Maya from Redwood, Liam's with me for the deep perf bits and Noah will cover the orchestration notes. Aria, Samir, welcome.
[00:18] Aria Gomez: hey thanks, quick note we're on a tight runway so trying to validate steadystate numbers this week.
[00:25] Maya Chen: totally — today's plan: quick run recap (last 72h), talk continuous batching tweaks we pushed, re-evaluate concurrency targets per GPU, queueing/backpressure observations, then agree weekend stress test and owners. sound good?
[00:40] Samir Rao: yes. also we'll surface a couple infra questions re: private vs hosted traffic shaping.
[00:48] Liam Patel: cool, jumping in with the run recap. we ran three profiles in the last 72 hours: steady 400 rps small prompts, bursty 1k-1.6k rps spikes, and mixed long prompt heavy traces. aggregate: steady 400 rps achieved with p95 latency ~420ms, p99 ~890ms; burst profiles hit peaks ~1.5k rps but tail jumped to ~1.6s p95 due to cold KV cache misses and queuing spikes.
[01:20] Lena Ortiz: wait 1.6 seconds p95? for which model/config?
[01:25] Liam Patel: that's for the 13B quantized model on dedicated r5g-gpu nodes with continuous batching enabled at default buffer 20ms/32 req. when cache warmed up, latencies dropped to ~350ms p95. Cold starts and prefix cache misses caused the spike.
[01:44] Aria Gomez: K/V cache — I heard K-V cash earlier in past notes — can you explain the miss behavior?
[01:51] Liam Patel: sure; KV cache miss meaning the prefix we expected to hit wasn't in memory for that worker, so the request either goes to a different shard or incurs a slow path re-load. in our topology we saw a 73% hit-rate on short prompts, 42% on long contexts. Samir, you had a note about tokenization differences?
[02:10] Samir Rao: yeah a couple prompts in our prod trace include expanded system messages which push context length — that reduces cache hits. we can trim system prefixes or use prefix normalization to improve hits.
[02:24] Noah Rivera: aside: when cache warms we also observed smarter batching packing more small requests into micro-batches which improves throughput but can increase p95 slightly since we hold a few ms to wait for batch fill.
[02:36] Maya Chen: right — it's the classic latency vs cost/throughput trade. we tuned continuous batching to be more aggressive this run: buffer down from 20ms to 12ms and max batch size from 32 to 48 in the high-throughput lanes. result: steady-state RPS up ~28% and CPU/GPU utilization smoother, but cold-hit tails still problematic.
[02:58] Diego Park: numbers — what was the new steady RPS?
[03:02] Liam Patel: for that config steady moved from ~3,000 rpm to ~3,850 rpm on a 4-GPU pool (that's requests per minute), for short prompts median latency stayed ~120ms tokens/time but p95 on short windows 380-420ms.
[03:20] Aria Gomez: can you translate rpm to concurrency per GPU? our infra team thinks in concurrency.
[03:26] Liam Patel: sure — roughly that equates to 8-10 active concurrency per GPU for short prompts given your average token lengths. we recommend targeting a ceiling of 12 concurrency per GPU for the pilot to tolerate bursts, then use queue shaping to protect latency SLOs.
[03:45] Samir Rao: 12 seems high — worried about memory pressure on quantized models. any OOM saw?
[03:50] Liam Patel: we observed one OOM on a node during long prompt heavy test — caused by ephemeral peak when three long-context requests landed on same worker. mitigation: shard affinity + smarter placement and slightly lower concurrency for long-context lanes (4-6).
[04:09] Maya Chen: that's why we split lanes: short-prompt lane (higher concurrency target), long-prompt lane (lower concurrency). queue depth and backpressure also matter. we instrumented the queue depth histogram — saw pronounced queues at 20-30 requests when burst hits; we propose lowering queue depth to 12 for short-prompt lane and 6 for long-prompt lane.
[04:32] Lena Ortiz: lowering queue depth means more rejects or retries upstream? our app can't silently drop requests.
[04:38] Maya Chen: correct — instead of drop we recommend 429 + client-side retry with jitter, or graceful fallback to smaller model tier for non-critical requests. also Redwood supports prioritization so you can protect interactive routes.
[04:51] Aria Gomez: interesting. how did fallbacks behave in the tests?
[04:55] Liam Patel: fallbacks to a smaller 6B variant reduced p95 by ~40% during spikes but increased cost due to duplicate token generation if client retries immediately. best path is routing + smart backoff.
[05:10] Samir Rao: regarding routing — can you do region-aware fallbacks? our EU traffic is sensitive to residency.
[05:16] Noah Rivera: yes we can route by policy; for EU we can pin to EU region pools and have fallback within same region to comply with residency.
[05:23] Aria Gomez: ok good. next, burst capacity — we saw transient throttle events — what triggers Redwood's burst cap?
[05:31] Liam Patel: burst capacity is configured per dedicated pool. in your pilot it's 20% burst over committed baseline; we hit that around 02:00 UTC during the test and saw queueing because new workers boot time added. recommended: enable warm standby / faster scale-up or pre-warm a small buffer for expected stress windows.
[05:51] Maya Chen: action item: we'll send a pre-warm checklist, and a playbook for scale-up behavior.
[05:58] Aria Gomez: perf heatmap — can we see which endpoints contribute most to tail?
[06:03] Liam Patel: yes — we instrumented per-route latencies. the reorder endpoint (product search rerank) drives most long-context hits because we feed in 1.2k token histories. If you can do prefix compaction there will be big wins.
[06:19] Samir Rao: we can look at compaction, but that requires product changes. is there an interim config to help?
[06:24] Liam Patel: yes drop concurrency for that route and route it to the long-prompt lane; also increase KV cache retention for that route to keep prefixes in memory longer (cost tradeoff).
[06:36] Maya Chen: ok agreed. now the weekend stress test — Liam?
[06:40] Liam Patel: plan is a 6-hour window Aug 14 (midnight-6am UTC) we will replay two traces: steady high-throughput and bursty shopping event mix. objectives: validate p95 under sustained 4k rpm for 4 hours, validate auto-scaling thresholds and warm standby, and confirm no OOMs. we will run with the tuned batching config (12ms buffer, max batch 48) and split lanes as discussed.
[07:04] Aria Gomez: can Redwood collect flame graphs or perf traces we can ingest?
[07:08] Noah Rivera: yes we'll export perf traces, batch histograms, and a room-level heatmap to the shared folder. note: traces may include redacted user data — we'll anonymize as agreed.
[07:18] Diego Park: pricing concern — if we run bigger burst capacity and warm standby, how much uplift?
[07:23] Maya Chen: at pilot scale the incremental cost for a 20% warm standby is roughly a 12-15% uplift on committed spend; we'll share a pro forma. also continuous batching reduces per-token cost, offsetting some of that.
[07:36] Samir Rao: any risk of quality regression with more aggressive batching? we've seen prompt interleaving issues before.
[07:42] Liam Patel: model-level correctness is unaffected — interleaving is within request boundaries. but if you rely on exact timing for external tool calls there's slight jitter. we tested function-calling flows, all OK but we'll push a targeted eval set across the weekend run.
[07:57] Aria Gomez: good. quick question about monitoring — what dashboards will we get?
[08:02] Noah Rivera: per-route latency, batch size distribution, KV cache hit-rate, queue depth histograms, GPU utilization, scaling events and fallback events. we can add custom alerts for p95>500ms or queue depth>15.
[08:16] Lena Ortiz: set alert for queue depth>10 for short lane.
[08:19] Maya Chen: noted.
[08:21] Samir Rao: we still have the one OOM — any short term mitigation beyond placement? maybe cap concurrency at 10?
[08:27] Liam Patel: cap concurrency at 10 for short lane, 5 for long lane; add shard affinity so same user's long-context requests don't land on same worker; also increase kv cache retention for top 10 prefixes we identified.
[08:41] Aria Gomez: sounds like a plan. recapping next steps and owners?
[08:44] Maya Chen: recap: Maya shares tuned runbook and batching configs by Aug 12; Liam runs the stress test Aug 14 and sends playbook Aug 13; Samir uploads traces by Aug 11; Lena validates egress/burst limits by Aug 13. Aria to confirm Aug 18 stakeholder meeting.
[09:01] Diego Park: will you include suggested client retry windows? we prefer guidelines.
[09:05] Noah Rivera: yes — recommended 300-700ms initial jittered backoff for 429s, exponential up to 2s. we'll include examples.
[09:13] Maya Chen: any other risks?
[09:15] Samir Rao: only compliance check — we will run EU traces in EU region, confirm data residency.
[09:20] Maya Chen: ok we'll ensure routing policy pinned.
[09:23] Aria Gomez: ok thanks everyone — this was useful.
[09:26] Maya Chen: thanks all. we'll follow up with docs and schedule.

Meeting end.
